---
title: "Quiz: docking by correlation"
---

Short questions to test your understanding. Try each on paper first, then open the answer. The receptor grid holds 1 on a thin surface layer around the receptor and $\rho < 0$ in its core; the ligand grid holds 1 on its cells; the score of a pose is the sum of the receptor grid under the ligand.

---

**Q1.** What do the surface layer and the core each contribute to the score, and why is $\rho$ large and negative?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
What should happen to a pose in which the ligand pushes into the receptor?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Every ligand cell on the surface layer adds 1: it rewards **contact**. Every ligand cell in the core adds $\rho$: it punishes **overlap** (a clash). With $\rho = -9$ one clash cancels nine contacts, so poses that overlap lose against poses that only touch; the score in effect forbids overlap and then counts contact.
:::

---

**Q2.** Why can one FFT give the score of every shift of the ligand, but not of every angle?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Write the score of a shift as a sum. What does turning the ligand do to its grid?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
For a fixed angle the score is $\sum_x a(x)\,b(x - d)$, a correlation of the two grids in the shift $d$, and the correlation theorem computes all shifts with FFTs. A turn is not a shift of the ligand's grid: the grid has to be made again for every angle (turned and rasterised), so the angles need a loop, one correlation each.
:::

---

**Q3.** Which FFTs are computed once, and which once per angle?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Which of the two molecules is turned?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
The receptor's FFT is computed once (it never moves). For each angle: the FFT of the turned ligand and one inverse FFT of the product. With $R$ angles: $1 + 2R$ FFTs, e.g. 145 for 72 angles.
:::

---

**Q4.** Why are both grids zero-padded before the FFT?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
The FFT correlation is circular.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
The DFT treats the grid as repeating: a ligand pushed past the right border reappears on the left. Without padding it could "touch" or "clash with" the receptor through the border. With the receptor in the middle of a grid that leaves a margin at least as wide as the ligand on every side, the wrapped part lands in empty space (as with linear correlation on the FFT registration day).
:::

---

**Q5.** You set $\rho = -0.1$. What happens to the best pose, and why?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
What does a ligand gain and lose by moving into the receptor?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Overlap now costs almost nothing, so the ligand **sinks in** wherever that brings more of its cells onto the surface layer. In the demo the best pose has 67 contacts and 44 clashes, at a wrong angle, and the true fit drops to second place.
:::

---

**Q6.** The angle step is 30° and the true fit is at 20°. Why can the search miss it, although 20° is only 10° from a searched angle?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
How far does a point of the ligand move when it turns by 10°, compared with the gap in the pocket?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
A turn of 10° moves a point at distance $r$ from the centre by about $r \cdot 10\pi/180 \approx 0.17r$: for a point 10 grid cells away, almost 2 cells. A tight pocket has a clearance of less than a cell, so at 30° (and at 0°) the key clashes and the true pose scores badly. The step must be small compared with (clearance / ligand radius).
:::

---

**Q7.** Why do docking pipelines keep thousands of poses from the FFT search instead of only the best one?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
What does the grid score leave out?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
The score is coarse: the molecules are treated as rigid, the grid is coarse, the energy is a crude count. The true pose often has a few clashes (side chains and loops move on binding) and need not be the top-scoring one. Keeping many poses and **re-ranking** them with finer models (clustering, energy refinement, flexibility) catches it.
:::

---

**Q8.** About how many ligand orientations does a 3D search with 6° steps need, and why not just three nested loops over angles in 6° steps?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
$8\pi^2/\Delta\theta^3$ with $\Delta\theta$ in radians. What happens to Euler-angle samples near the poles?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
$8\pi^2/(0.105)^3 \approx 69\,000$ orientations. Three nested loops over Euler angles give $60 \cdot 30 \cdot 60 \approx 108\,000$ samples, unevenly spread: near the poles many of them are almost the same rotation, elsewhere they are too far apart. Even samplings spread directions over the sphere and add turns about each.
:::

---

**Q9.** *(math)* The receptor is $a = s_R + i\,c_R$ and the ligand $b = s_L - i\,c_L$ (surface layers $s$, cores $c$). Show that the real part of $\sum_x a(x)\,\overline{b(x - d)}$ is "surface·surface − core·core".

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
$\overline{s_L - i\,c_L} = s_L + i\,c_L$; multiply out.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
$(s_R + i c_R)(s_L + i c_L) = s_R s_L - c_R c_L + i\,(s_R c_L + c_R s_L)$. Summed over $x$ (with $s_L, c_L$ at $x - d$), the real part is $\sum s_R s_L - \sum c_R c_L$: contact of the two surface layers minus overlap of the two cores, in one complex correlation.
:::
